newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan car export surge to U.S. seen easing -- MITI.
newsitem.headline: Japan car export surge to U.S. seen easing -- MITI.

text.p: The present trend of increasing Japanese automotive exports to the United States is unlikely to continue unchanged, Japanese Vice Minister for International Trade Hisashi Hosokawa told Reuters on Tuesday.
"I do not think that the present auto export trend will continue in the same manner as we have seen in the first quarter of the year," Hosokawa said in an interview.
"So in total, if you look at 1997 as a whole, I think in effect that Japanese exports, particularly to the United States, will not be that worrisome," he said.

U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said last Friday that she was worried by trade trends that began to develop in late 1996 and early 1997, particularly a surge in Japanese car imports in the U.S. market during the first three months of 1997.
A U.S. trade official told reporters then that if Japan's trade surplus continued to rise significantly, tensions between the two countries were bound to increase.
Hosokawa said on Tuesday that Japanese car makers' plans to increase production in the U.S. later this year would be one factor altering the recent export trend.

Hosokawa also said trade and economic issues were likely to come up when U.S. President Bill Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto meet later this week, but they were not expected to dominate the talks.
"The coming summit meeting...will most likely focus on the political side and security-related issues, but I don't deny that they will also discuss to some extent economic issues," he said.
"That is my prediction -- it's totally up to them -- and yet in light of the present environment surrounding the heads of the two countries, that is my view," he added.
U.S. officials have recently been warning Japan against letting its trade surplus surge again and urging Tokyo to take steps to ensure its recovery is led by domestic demand, not exports.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said on Monday that Clinton and Hashimoto would talk about the need for Japan to increase demand for imports from the United States and that there would be "some discussion of trade issues" at the talks.
Hosokawa also said it would be reasonable to assume that Hashimoto would affirm his commitment to deregulate Japan's economy when he met Clinton.

"Logically, a deregulation programme should be of great help to imports to the Japanese market," he said, adding that Hashimoto was "firmly determined" to carrying out economic reforms including deregulation.

Hosokawa, referring to the present yen/dollar exchange rate, said some firms might feel that the weak yen was reducing pressure on them to restructure. "In light of the present yen rate, some companies may well find it easier to be competitive, and yet they need to be further restructured," he said. "However, in the present environment, such (restructuring) spirit, I'm afraid, might be somewhat lessened."
